lessons.title: An artist uses line and colour
lessons.outcome: Find out about an artist who expresses feelings.
lessons.goal: I can find out how an artist uses line and colour.
success: I can name the artist or point to his name.
I can find two facts in the short description.
I can try my own idea with shapes.
words: A space with an edge, such as a circle.
Put things where you want them.

artist_cards.description: Henri Matisse made art with line, colour and cut paper. He used line and colour to show feelings. He cut shapes from painted paper. He moved the shapes to try a new layout. We can read his art in our own way. We do not know his mood from it.
artist_cards.notice: What did he cut? What could he move?
artist_cards.prompt: How could moving your own shapes change the way your piece feels?
artist_cards.model_answer: He cut shapes from painted paper and moved the shapes to try a layout. In my own art, I could move shapes apart to suggest calm, or put them close to suggest energy. Those are my own readings. They do not tell us what he felt.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Today we find out about one real artist.
You can point, speak, sign or pass.
Our own art can use a made-up feeling.
stages.say: An artist makes art. Today the artist is Henri Matisse. Say the name slowly, or point to it while I read it. We will use a short description, not a copy of his artwork. You may use an invented feeling for your own response and share privately.
stages.good: The pupil can indicate the artist's name or recognise it when read aloud. No personal disclosure or public performance is required.
stages.fallback: Read the name aloud and let the pupil confirm it with an agreed gesture. No print, image or art materials are needed.
stages.answer: Naming, pointing to or confirming the spoken name is acceptable. A pupil does not need to spell the name from memory.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Watch a curved air line, then a sharp air line.
What do you notice?
Could each line suggest a feeling? You may have your own view.
stages.say: I make a slow curve in the air, then a sharp zigzag. Tell me one thing you notice before guessing a feeling. A curve might suggest calm to me. You might read it differently. We do not know a maker's private mood from one line.
stages.good: The pupil notices a visible feature and distinguishes it from an interpretation, with support if needed.
stages.fallback: Describe the two lines aloud or follow the pupil's directions. A pupil can watch without making a movement.
stages.answer: The curve bends smoothly; the zigzag changes direction sharply. A feeling linked to either feature is a possible reading, not a fixed rule.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Listen to the short artist description.
Find two facts: cut shapes and moved shapes.
Watch the adult try two new layouts.
These class tests are our own work.
stages.say: Read the artist card aloud in short parts. Matisse used line and colour to express feelings. In his cut-paper work he cut painted paper and could change the layout. Those are facts from the description. I now use my own three torn shapes. I place them close, then move them apart. I think the wider space feels calm. That last idea is my reading. These shapes and this design are an original class example, not a copy of his art.
stages.good: The adult identifies two accurate details and models the difference between a fact and a personal interpretation. The original class sample uses a general method while retaining its own design.
stages.fallback: Read the description aloud. Use three finger positions close together, then apart, or describe those positions. A pupil may direct the adult's hand positions.
stages.answer: Ask: 'Which is a fact from the card: he moved cut shapes, or everyone must feel calm?' Expected: he moved cut shapes. If unclear, reread that sentence and point to the original class shapes.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help place three class shapes.
Try them close, then far apart.
Say what changed. Choose a layout for a made-up feeling.
Finish: This suggests ___ to me.
stages.say: You direct our own class sample. We keep the shapes the same and change their spacing. What do you notice? Which layout could fit your invented feeling? Hinge: A pupil says all blue shapes must mean sad. Do we A accept one fixed meaning, or B ask the maker for their meaning and reason?
stages.good: The pupil compares two layouts and gives or confirms a reason linked to spacing. The pupil recognises that a colour does not have one compulsory emotional meaning.
stages.fallback: Direct three adult finger positions or listen to two spoken layouts. Choose verbally or with an agreed gesture.
stages.answer: B. Ask the maker. If a pupil selects A, model two different readings of the same blue shape. Parallel check: 'Could a blue shape show joy to its maker?' Expected: yes, if that is their intended meaning. Move on when the pupil can identify a feature and allow another reading.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, name the artist.
Keep two facts from the description.
Make or draw three shapes of your own.
Try two layouts. Choose one for a made-up feeling.
Keep your tests and your own reason.
stages.say: Choose drawing, torn paper or a silent route. For torn paper, make three simple shapes from scrap. Tearing is enough; no cutting tool is needed. Try the shapes close together and farther apart before fixing anything. For drawing, make two tiny versions on scrap. For a sound response, try three quiet taps close in time, then with wider pauses; this changes space in time in your own art form. Keep sound below talking volume and stop on my raised hand. The pupil decides the feeling and layout. Do not recreate an existing artwork. An adult may handle materials under the pupil's direction.
stages.good: The pupil retains two real artist details, makes two original trials and chooses a layout or sequence with a reason. A simple test is enough today. Staff distinguish the artist facts, the pupil's view and the adult's observation.
stages.fallback: Use or direct three silent hand positions close, then apart. The pupil names or confirms the artist and two spoken facts. The adult records the actual sequence and confirmed pupil reason when a recording method is available.
stages.answer: Example only: Matisse cut painted paper and moved shapes. I tried three own shapes close and apart. I chose apart because it feels calm to me. This is the pupil's possible method link, not a claim about the artist's mood.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Tell an adult one fact about the artist.
Show your two tests and chosen layout.
Say: I chose ___ because ___.
Tidy and keep your work for next time.
stages.say: Ask for an artist fact first, then the pupil's own view. A listener describes one feature before offering a different interpretation. The maker can keep their choice. Sharing may be private. Use the last two minutes to cap glue, collect scraps and store loose shapes and tests flat in each pupil's own tray.
stages.good: The pupil separates an accurate artist detail from a personal interpretation. The trials and chosen layout are retained honestly for lesson two.
stages.fallback: The pupil directs a repeat of their silent layout. The adult repeats one fact and asks the pupil to confirm or correct it, then records the pupil's own choice.
stages.answer: A useful artist fact is that he moved cut shapes to test a layout. A personal view is that a pupil's wide gaps seem calm. Both belong in the log with their different purposes clear.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: The artist is ___.
Two facts I found are ___ and ___.
My own test used ___.
I chose ___ because ___.
stages.say: Keep the actual artist facts and your own work separate in the log. I can scribe your words, read them back and let you correct them. Use today's real date and record the help used. Keep your own tests so you can make a short response next time.
stages.good: A dated entry gives or confirms the artist's name, two facts, a pupil-made trial and a chosen feature with a reason. No adult example is prefilled as pupil evidence.
stages.fallback: Use an oral log. The adult confirms the name, facts and choice with the pupil, then makes a dated witness note at the next recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: The artist is Henri Matisse. He cut painted paper and moved shapes. I tried three own shapes apart. I chose wide gaps because they feel calm to me.

Supported: Listen to the artist card with an adult.
Point to or say cut shapes and moved shapes.
Try three own shapes close, then apart.
Choose a layout. Tell or show your reason.
Independent: Name the artist and find two facts.
Make two new trials with your own shapes.
Choose a layout for a made-up feeling.
Add the facts, tests and reason to your arts log.
Aspire: Complete the two trials and artist facts.
Try one new gap or line in your own design.
Say how it changes your reading.
Keep your own view and allow a different view.

log: Two facts I found are ___ and ___.
misconceptions: An artist's work tells us exactly how they felt
A description can give facts about a method. A feeling suggested to a viewer is an interpretation, not proof of a private mood.
To learn from an artist we must copy their picture
Use a general method, such as moving shapes, then make an original design with the pupil's own shapes and arrangement.
A colour always means one feeling
Ask the maker for their intended meaning and a reason. Different personal and cultural readings are valid.
kit: For four pupils: four books or arts logs, four pencils and eight small test sheets.
Paper route: twelve ready-torn scrap shapes plus spare scrap paper, four mats and two glue sticks. Keep shapes loose until a layout is chosen. No cutting tool is required.
Drawing route: four sets of familiar drawing tools. Optional paint uses five brushes, four mats, two stable water pots, a small shared amount of washable paint and cloths.
Adult model: three original torn shapes and two different arrangements. Label them as original class examples. Do not display or copy an actual artist's work.
Quiet sound route: fingertips only, below talking volume. Materials-free route: silent hand positions or pupil-directed adult movement. Keep four labelled storage spaces for actual trials.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Read the artist name and two short facts. Say: He cut painted paper and moved the shapes.
15 to 30 seconds
Place three own torn shapes close together. Say: These are our new class shapes, not a copy of his work.
30 to 45 seconds
Move the same shapes apart. Say: I changed the spacing. This layout feels calm to me. That is my reading.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the two tests. Say: I keep the artist fact, my own test and my reason as separate parts of my log.
models: Teacher model only: Matisse cut painted paper and moved shapes. I used the idea of moving my own shapes. I chose wide gaps because they suggest calm to me.
Teacher model only: I kept the same three shapes and changed their spacing. Someone else may read my piece in a different way. The artist's private mood is not known from our description.

lessons.title: My own response to an artist
lessons.outcome: Find out about an artist who expresses feelings.
lessons.goal: I can link my own art to an artist's idea.
success: I can recall two facts about the artist.
I can make my own piece using a new layout.
I can say how the artist's idea helped me.
words: A space with an edge, such as a circle.
Your own work made after you explore an idea.

artist_cards.description: Henri Matisse made art with line, colour and cut paper. He used line and colour to show feelings. He cut shapes from painted paper. He moved the shapes to try a new layout. We can read his art in our own way. We do not know his mood from it.
artist_cards.notice: What did he cut? What could he move?
artist_cards.prompt: How could moving your own shapes change the way your piece feels?
artist_cards.model_answer: He cut shapes from painted paper and moved the shapes to try a layout. In my own art, I could move shapes apart to suggest calm, or put them close to suggest energy. Those are my own readings. They do not tell us what he felt.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your real trials from last time.
Listen to the artist card again if needed.
Tell or show one fact and your chosen layout.
stages.say: Find your own tests. If you were away or the tests are missing, hear the short card and make a quick fresh trial now. We use today's real date. Matisse is the artist; the new response will belong to you. You may use an invented feeling and share privately.
stages.good: The pupil identifies an actual prior choice or makes an honest catch-up trial, and recalls an artist detail with rereading if needed.
stages.fallback: Read the card aloud and offer three silent hand positions close, then apart. The pupil chooses one or directs a new layout.
stages.answer: A fresh trial and a reread card are valid. Do not invent a previous piece, quotation or pupil response.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Which are facts from the artist card?
Cut painted paper. Moved the shapes.
Does a shape tell us the artist's private mood?
stages.say: Ask the pupil to name or point to two facts: cut painted paper and moved shapes. Then ask whether our description tells us exactly how he felt. A viewer can have a personal reading while being honest about what the facts show.
stages.good: The pupil identifies or confirms two accurate method details and knows that the description does not prove a private emotional state.
stages.fallback: Give one spoken fact at a time and use an agreed yes or no gesture. Allow the pupil to listen again before responding.
stages.answer: Both method details are facts in the card. No, a shape alone does not tell us the artist's private mood. Reread and model one fact versus one personal reading if needed.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch the adult use an artist's idea in a new way.
Move three own shapes. Choose a new layout.
Make a small piece for a made-up feeling.
Say what is the artist link and what is your own choice.
stages.say: Matisse's method of trying arrangements helped me. I use my own three torn shapes and move them into a rising path. I choose this layout for an invented feeling of hope. My shapes and layout are my own design. I may draw round them or use a little glue under each shape once I choose. I do not recreate an existing composition. In a silent response I can place three hand shapes low, middle and high. I explain the method link without pretending the artist made my piece.
stages.good: The adult makes an original short response and clearly separates a general borrowed method from the new subject, shapes, arrangement and interpretation.
stages.fallback: Use or direct three silent hand shapes at different heights, or describe their order. A pupil who prefers stillness can make every choice verbally.
stages.answer: Ask: 'Which came from learning about the artist: moving shapes to test a layout, or my exact new shape path?' Expected: the method of testing a layout. The exact path is the adult's own example.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help make one new class response.
Choose a layout and a made-up feeling.
Check the artist link and our own choices.
Finish: The artist's idea helped us ___.
stages.say: You direct our original shapes. We can change spacing, line or position for our own idea. Hinge: Which is an honest log: A 'I made the artist's real work', or B 'I tried moving my own shapes after hearing about his method'? Ask why the record is honest.
stages.good: The pupil makes an intentional new choice and distinguishes an original response from a copied or falsely attributed artwork.
stages.fallback: Use a pupil-directed silent sequence or spoken layout. Ask the same A or B question orally and let the pupil confirm a choice.
stages.answer: B is honest. If a pupil chooses A, point out the different maker, shapes and layout. Parallel check: 'Can I write my own name or code on my own response and name the artist as the idea link?' Expected: yes. Continue when the pupil can identify the method link and their own choice.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, use your real test.
Make a small piece with your own shapes or moves.
Choose a layout for a made-up feeling.
Check one part. Keep or change it for a reason.
Add the artist link and your own words.
stages.say: Use your selected trial or choose a fresh layout and record why. For paper art, move three own torn shapes before fixing. Use a little glue underneath, press gently on the mat and keep fingers clear of wet paint. Drawing is equally valid. For a sound response, choose three soft taps with your own pauses and order; the link is testing spacing in your own form. Keep sound below talking volume and stop on a raised hand. A small piece is enough. An adult may handle materials under the pupil's direction. The pupil decides the feeling, layout and review.
stages.good: A real original response, two accurate artist details recalled with support if needed, and a clear link from the artist's general method to a pupil-owned feature. The log distinguishes intention and observation. Record unfinished work honestly rather than claiming a final piece.
stages.fallback: Make or direct a silent layout or movement response, or give an original spoken description. The adult records the actual ordered actions, the pupil's stated emotion, artist link and decision when a recording method is available.
stages.answer: Example only: I moved my own shapes, as the description said the artist could do. My layout rises because I chose hope. I kept the space at the end because it seems open to me. A different reason or art form is valid.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show an adult or partner your own response.
Name the artist and the idea that helped you.
Say: My own choice was ___ because ___.
Tidy and keep the response with your log.
stages.say: Ask for the artist link and a choice in the actual response. A listener can notice a feature and offer a different reading. The maker decides what to keep. Sharing can be private. Use the last two minutes to cap glue, return tools, collect scraps and store work flat. Keep the real response, trials and log together.
stages.good: The pupil explains a method link and a personal choice without claiming the class models or their response are works by the artist. Tools and evidence are stored safely.
stages.fallback: Witness a silent response privately and read a short factual description back for the pupil to confirm. Keep the pupil's interpretation separate from the adult's observed actions.
stages.answer: A useful review is 'The artist moved shapes to test a layout. I moved my own shapes apart because I wanted calm.' It does not need to tell a personal life story.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: The artist is ___.
I found out ___ and ___.
The artist's idea helped me ___.
My own choice was ___ because ___.
stages.say: Keep the artist facts and the response in their proper roles. Ask the pupil what they found out and how it helped their own work. Scribe exact words if needed, read them back and allow correction. Use the actual date, help used and true state of the work. This entry contributes to the ongoing Explore log.
stages.good: A dated log gives or confirms the artist name, two facts, an original response or witnessed sequence, and a method link with a personal choice and reason. No quotation or model answer is passed off as pupil evidence.
stages.fallback: Take an oral log with agreed gestures or a spoken description. The adult records only the actual confirmed facts, response and pupil words at the next recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: The artist is Henri Matisse. He cut painted paper and moved shapes. His idea helped me test a layout. I chose a rising path because it suggests hope to me.

Supported: Hear the card again. Find the two facts.
Choose a real test or make one now.
Make or direct your own small response.
Tell an adult the artist link and your choice.
Independent: Recall two facts about the artist.
Use a test to make your own small piece.
Keep or change one part for a reason.
Log the method link and your own choice.
Aspire: Complete your own response and log.
Try one new layout with the same shapes.
Say which layout best fits your idea and why.
Explain a different way someone could read it.

log: My work or witness note is ___.
misconceptions: An original response must look like the artist's actual work
Borrow a general method such as testing a layout, then use the pupil's own shapes, arrangement, subject and reason.
The teacher decides the feeling in the pupil's piece
The maker names or confirms the intended emotion. An adult supports access and records the pupil's own explanation.
The log can describe work that we meant to make
Retain actual work or a precise witness note. State the true stage and next step; do not invent a finished piece or earlier trial.
kit: For four pupils: four real trial sets, four books or arts logs, four pencils and eight small scrap pieces for fresh trials if needed.
Paper route: twelve pupil-owned torn shapes or scrap to tear, four small bases, four mats and two glue sticks. Shapes can stay loose until a layout is chosen. No cutting tool is required.
Drawing route: four sets of familiar drawing tools. Optional paint uses five brushes, four mats, two stable water pots, a little washable paint and cloths.
Adult model: three original shapes and a new layout based on the method of trying arrangements. The artist card is read aloud; no actual artwork is displayed or copied.

Quiet sound needs only fingertips; the materials-free route uses silent hand positions, pupil-directed adult movement or an original spoken description. Keep four individual storage places and a flat drying area.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Point to two facts from the artist description. Say: He cut painted paper and moved shapes. That helps me think about a method.
15 to 30 seconds
Move three own torn shapes into a new path. Say: I test my own layout for an invented feeling of hope.
30 to 45 seconds
Keep or change a gap and fix only when chosen. Or show a silent low-middle-high hand sequence. Say: My choices and this new design are my own.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the actual response. Say: The artist's idea helped me test a layout. I keep that link and my own reason in my log.
models: Teacher model only: Matisse moved cut shapes to test a layout. That helped me move my own shapes before fixing them. I chose a rising path because it suggests hope to me.
Teacher model only: I made a silent hand response with a wide gap at the end. The artist's method gave me the idea to test spacing. My sequence and intended feeling are my own.

lessons.title: Two ideas for resilience
lessons.outcome: Plan an artwork on the theme of resilience.
lessons.goal: I can plan two different ideas and choose one for a reason.
success: I can make two small rough plans.
I can show how each idea links to resilience.
I can choose one idea and give a reason.
words: Finding a way forward. This can include a pause, help or a new method.
A record of what you want to make and how.
A small rough sketch of an idea.
A short note that explains a part.
Something you pick for a reason.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Choose visual art, sound or silent movement.
Use a made-up idea. You may share privately.
stages.say: We are planning an original artwork about resilience. It can show a pause, a new route or help. It does not need a story from your life. Choose visual art, a quiet sound idea or a silent movement idea. You can plan by speaking, drawing, signing or directing me.
stages.good: The pupil chooses or indicates a form and understands that today's work is planning. An invented or abstract idea is accepted. Quiet and private routes are available.
stages.fallback: Pupil speaks or directs an adult to describe a four-part sequence. Stillness, silent movement or an adult-scribed plan are valid.
stages.answer: There is no preferred art form. The plan should show an intention through a feature or sequence.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Think of a seed after wind, a path round a block, or a pattern that returns.
Which might show a way forward? Give a reason.
stages.say: A seed could bend then grow in a new direction. A path could find a way around a block. A pattern could stop for a gap, then return. These are made-up possibilities, not fixed meanings. Which one gives you an idea, and why? You may choose another idea.
stages.good: The pupil links a possible subject or abstract feature to finding a way forward. The adult accepts a reasoned different interpretation and does not infer a private feeling.
stages.fallback: Read the choices aloud. Pupil chooses a spoken option or directs one small gesture. No image or materials are needed.
stages.answer: For example: A path around a block could show finding another way. A returning pattern could show starting again after a pause.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch two genuinely different rough plans.
See a picture plan and a short sequence plan.
A rough plan is enough today.
stages.say: My first rough idea shows a small seed bending, then a tall curve growing another way. My second shows a path turning around a block. They have different subjects and layouts. For sound or movement, I could plan four parts: repeat, pause, change, return. I label what the feature is meant to suggest. These are adult plans, not finished artwork or your evidence.
stages.good: The adult models two distinct options and a short label linking a feature to resilience. A small sketch, spoken sequence or four-part notation is enough. Pupils see that a plan need not be neat.
stages.fallback: Describe both ideas aloud or demonstrate the short sequence with small silent gestures. An adult can draw or note the pupil's directed layout.
stages.answer: Check: Are the plans different only because one is blue? No. A new subject, layout or sequence creates a real choice. If unclear, compare a seed plan with a path plan and identify one difference.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Compare two class plans.
Say what is different and what each could suggest.
Which one can be made with simple tools or no tools?
stages.say: Let us compare an invented seed plan and a returning-pattern plan. What is different? What could each suggest? Hinge: which pair gives a real choice? A the same layout in two colours, B a seed changing direction and a path around a block, or C two copies of the same plan. Explain your choice.
stages.good: The pupil chooses B and names a difference in subject or arrangement. They can explain a possible resilience link and notice one practical constraint. The adult models one comparison, then returns the choice.
stages.fallback: Read the options aloud. Pupil may point, sign, speak or direct the adult to outline the two plans in the air.
stages.answer: If A or C is chosen, name the repeated layout and model the different subject. Parallel check: Does a four-part pause-and-return sequence offer a different idea from a rising seed drawing? Yes. Continue when the pupil identifies one meaningful difference.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Make two small rough plans in your chosen form.
Use different subjects, layouts or sequences.
Add a short note to show what each idea means.
Choose one plan and say why.
stages.say: Plan two different ideas. Use small thumbnails for a picture, or a short ordered note for sound or movement. Keep the work rough and small. Label the feature that could show resilience. Choose one idea because it fits your intention and can be made with the access, time and materials available. This is a planning session, not the full making.
stages.good: Two genuine options are retained, each with an intention or resilience link. The pupil selects one for a specific reason. A directed or scribed plan preserves the pupil's decisions. No finished artwork is claimed.
stages.fallback: Pupil describes two original short sequences or directs an adult to show them. Adult keeps ordered notes and the exact confirmed choice and reason when a recording surface is available.
stages.answer: A useful reason links intention and feasibility: I choose the returning pattern because the pause shows a restart and I can make it with silent actions. A third plan is optional if it helps a decision.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show your two plans to an adult or partner.
Ask what they notice. You choose what to keep.
Keep both plans and your reason.
stages.say: The listener says one feature they notice, then asks what the maker intends. The maker can keep the choice or revise the reason after considering feedback. You may share with only me. Use the final two minutes to put tools away and store both rough plans for the next lesson.
stages.good: A pupil-owned decision remains clear after feedback. Both options and the selection reason are retained. Private sharing and an unchanged choice are valid.
stages.fallback: Adult reads both sequence notes back. Pupil confirms the choice or changes it. Note feedback separately from the pupil's decision.
stages.answer: Useful feedback: I notice the path turns around the block. The maker can explain why that matters. Do not require an audience to agree with the interpretation.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: My two ideas were ___.
I chose ___ because ___.
Next time my plan needs ___.
stages.say: Date the real planning work. Record the two ideas, your chosen plan, the feature you want to use and your reason. Add one thing the detailed plan will need next time. You can speak, sign, sketch or direct a scribe, and I will read your words back.
stages.good: A dated log records actual planning options and the pupil's own selection. The next step concerns developing the plan, not pretending the artwork has been made.
stages.fallback: Pupil gives an oral or gestured log. Adult retains the two precise idea notes and confirmed reason at the next available recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: My ideas were a seed and a returning rhythm. I chose the rhythm because the pause shows a restart. My next plan needs an ending.

Supported: Choose a picture or short sequence plan.
Make two small ideas with an adult if needed.
Point to what is different. Choose one.
Independent: Make two different small plans in your chosen form.
Label the feature that could show resilience.
Choose one idea. Explain why it fits your intention.
Keep both plans and your reason.
Aspire: Complete both rough plans and choose one.
Explain one strength and one limit of each idea.
Say why the chosen idea can be made with simple tools or no tools.
The next level task is optional.

log: Each idea could show resilience by ___.
The feature I will use is ___.
misconceptions: Resilience means never pausing or asking for help.
A pause, support or a different route can be part of finding a way forward. Use invented or abstract ideas, not personal hardship.
Two ideas must be almost the same design.
Change the main subject, arrangement or sequence so the plans offer a real choice. Changing only a colour may not make a genuinely different idea.
A plan is a finished artwork.
Keep rough sketches, labels or short sequence notes as plans. The full making happens later. Do not claim completed artwork this week.
A more complex idea is always better.
Choose an idea that communicates an intention and can be made with the time, space, materials and access available. A small original piece can work well.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and ten small planning spaces for two rough ideas each. Use a third space only if useful.
Optional visual route: six drawing tools including the adult model, five blank layout areas and a small set of colour tools for planning labels. No paint, cutting or fixing is required this week.
Sound or movement plans: five four-part sequence spaces, or five spoken/witness records. Fingertips and seated actions are enough for a brief planning demonstration.
Adult examples: two or three labelled original rough plans, one selected plan and one materials-and-time plan. These are teacher models, not pupil evidence.
For lesson two retain each pupil's chosen rough plan, reason and any feedback. No recording device or specialist art kit is required.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Say: I can plan a made-up idea. Show a small seed that bends, then grows another way. Label: change direction.
15 to 30 seconds
Show a separate path turning around a block. Say: This is a different subject and layout. Label: find another route.
30 to 45 seconds
Show four silent planned parts: repeat, pause, change, return. Say: A sequence note is a plan too.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to one option. Say: I choose this because it fits my idea and I can make it. I keep the other plan to show my choice.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Compare both plans. Note a strength and a limit of each. Think about time, tools or access. Explain why your choice fits the idea. Say what you will test in the detailed plan.
stretch.evidence: Keep both plans, your comparison, one practical limit and your choice with reasons.
stretch.why_optional: This task is extra. Your Explore work is complete without it. Keep the record in case your next level changes.
stretch.good: The pupil weighs intention against a practical constraint, compares real options and gives a reasoned choice without claiming completed making.
stretch.fallback: Adult asks the same prompts orally and retains ordered idea notes with the pupil's confirmed comparison and reason.

models: Teacher model only: My ideas were a seed changing direction and a path around a block. I chose the path because the turn could show finding another way. I can plan it with a few clear lines.
Teacher model only: I planned a steady rhythm and a pause-and-return rhythm. I chose the second because the pause could show a fresh start. I still need to plan how the piece will end.
lessons.cover: Read the invented idea choices aloud. Model two small, genuinely different rough plans and a selection reason. Pupils retain two options in their chosen form, label their intention and choose one. Use short sequence notes for sound or movement. Do not begin full artwork making. Keep both plans and the arts log for lesson two. Use the seven-stage timing and final two Review minutes for tidy-up.

lessons.title: My plan ready for making
lessons.outcome: Plan an artwork on the theme of resilience.
lessons.goal: I can develop my chosen plan and explain how I will make it.
success: I can label a layout or ordered sequence.
I can plan materials, access, steps and time.
I can use feedback to check what my plan still needs.
words: Finding a way forward. This can include a pause, help or a new method.
A record of what you want to make and how.
A small rough sketch of an idea.
A short note that explains a part.
Something you pick for a reason.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find the plan you chose and your reason.
Today you will develop the plan. Making comes later.
stages.say: Find your selected rough plan and the reason from Monday. Today we will make it clear enough to use in a later making lesson. If the plan is missing, make two tiny honest options now and choose one. Record today's real date rather than inventing an earlier plan.
stages.good: The pupil identifies an actual selected idea or makes a brief dated catch-up choice. They understand that the task is planning, not full artwork making.
stages.fallback: Read back the ordered idea note. Pupil may describe the chosen idea or direct an adult to show it with small silent gestures.
stages.answer: An honest fresh plan is valid. Keep the pupil's own intention and choice.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: What does your chosen feature mean?
What does another person need to know to help you make it?
stages.say: Say the feature you chose and what it could suggest. Imagine a helpful adult reading your plan later. What would they need to know about the layout or order, tools, space or finish? We will add notes, not ask them to guess your intention.
stages.good: The pupil identifies an intention and one missing practical detail. A different audience reading is allowed while the maker keeps control of the plan.
stages.fallback: Adult asks two spoken choices at a time, such as order or tools. Pupil points, signs or gives one short answer.
stages.answer: Useful missing detail: where a path turns, how many marks repeat, when a pause comes, which tools are needed, or how the sequence ends.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch a rough idea become a usable plan.
Notice labels, counted tools, ordered steps and a time plan.
A small plan can be clear.
stages.say: My path plan has labels: start, block, turn and new route. I note one small sheet and two colour tools. My steps are place the main lines, add the turn, then check the meaning. My draft first making period is five minutes to set up, twenty to make, ten to check or change, and five to tidy: forty minutes. For a silent sequence I need no art tools. I note a clear seated space, four ordered actions and a stop cue. Staff can adjust the draft schedule before making.
stages.good: The model connects intention, labelled layout or sequence, counted resources, access, ordered steps and a workable draft time plan. Pupils see a plan can stay simple. No artwork is claimed to be complete.
stages.fallback: Read the same plan aloud. Pupil may direct an adult to place imagined parts or state four sequence actions. Use an oral materials list, access choice and time plan.
stages.answer: Check: Is a list saying make it nice enough? No. A usable plan says what comes first, which resources or no-materials route is used, and how the maker will check and finish.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help check a class plan for missing details.
Add one label, step or resource note.
Keep the maker in charge of the idea.
stages.say: Our original plan says repeat, pause, change, return, but it does not say how to stop. Let us add an ending cue. Hinge: a plan has a title but no steps or tools. Should we A start full making and guess, B add the missing details before making, or C copy someone else's plan? Explain.
stages.good: The pupil selects B and adds a practical detail that supports the maker's intention. Feedback concerns clarity and feasibility rather than forcing a different idea.
stages.fallback: Use an oral four-part plan. Pupil directs the adult to insert one missing action, pause, access note or stop cue. Choose A, B or C aloud or by pointing.
stages.answer: If A or C is chosen, model the confusion from one missing step. Parallel check: If a silent plan has no ending cue, should we add a clear stop before the making lesson? Yes. Continue when the pupil identifies a useful detail.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Develop your chosen layout or sequence. Add short labels.
Count the tools you need, or choose a no-materials route.
List the steps, space, access choice and a draft time plan.
Say how you will check the meaning.
stages.say: Use the chosen idea, not a new full artwork. Add labels showing what the parts mean. Write or say the materials and quantities. For a silent piece, say no art tools and plan the space, actions and stop cue. Put making steps in order and choose a manageable first forty-minute schedule. Use the adult model if helpful. Note a quiet or supported access option. Check that the later making is possible, then keep the plan for next week.
stages.good: An annotated layout or ordered sequence, resource quantities or no-materials choice, space/access note, ordered steps, draft time budget and meaning check form a usable plan. Staff approve tools and space before later making. Any unfinished planning is labelled honestly.
stages.fallback: Pupil directs an adult through the layout or sequence and gives an oral tools/no-tools list, order, access and time plan. Adult retains exact confirmed notes. No materials or device are needed to participate.
stages.answer: A workable simple plan could use one sheet, two colour tools and three ordered steps. A silent plan could use four small seated actions, a raised-hand stop and no art tools. These are options, not compulsory designs.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Ask an adult or partner to read your plan back.
What is clear? What still needs a note?
You choose what to change. Keep the real plan.
stages.say: Read or say the plan as if you will use it later. The listener describes one clear detail and asks one practical question. The maker decides whether to add or keep a feature and explains why. Use the final two minutes to tidy and store the selected plan, earlier options and log together.
stages.good: The pupil checks the plan against intention and feasibility, considers feedback and retains ownership of a revision or reasoned decision to keep it. No full making or completed result is claimed.
stages.fallback: Adult reads the exact oral plan back. Pupil confirms it or directs one change. A private audience is enough.
stages.answer: Useful feedback: I know the four actions but not the ending cue. Useful response: I added a raised-hand stop so the ending is clear.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: My plan shows ___ through ___.
I need ___. First I will ___.
I kept or changed ___ because ___.
stages.say: Record the actual plan, resources or no-tools route, ordered actions and one next check before making. Say what feedback you considered and what you decided. You can draw, speak, sign or use a scribe. I will read your words back. If a detail still needs staff approval, state that rather than pretending the plan is ready.
stages.good: A dated log points to the real annotated plan or sequence and records a choice, practical next step and any remaining approval or missing detail. Explore planning is complete without optional stretch.
stages.fallback: Pupil confirms the oral plan and next step. Adult retains the precise sequence and practical notes with the pupil's exact words.
stages.answer: Example only: My plan shows finding a new route through a turning path. I need one sheet and two colour tools. I added a turn label because the listener asked where the path changes.

Supported: Use one heading at a time with an adult.
Add labels or ordered actions. Count tools, or say no tools.
Choose steps and time. Tell or show one next check.
Independent: Label your chosen layout or sequence.
Plan counted tools, space and access, or a no-tools route.
Put the making steps in order. Add a draft time plan.
Use feedback to check one detail. Keep your reason.
Aspire: Check how the plan fits your intended meaning.
Explain one choice about tools, time or access.
Consider a practical question and record your own decision.
The next level task is optional.

log: My materials and amounts, or no-tools route, are ___.
My steps and draft time plan are ___.
Before making I need to check ___.
misconceptions: Resilience means never pausing or asking for help.
A pause, support or a different route can be part of finding a way forward. Use invented or abstract ideas, not personal hardship.
Two ideas must be almost the same design.
Change the main subject, arrangement or sequence so the plans offer a real choice. Changing only a colour may not make a genuinely different idea.
A plan is a finished artwork.
Keep rough sketches, labels or short sequence notes as plans. The full making happens later. Do not claim completed artwork this week.
A more complex idea is always better.
Choose an idea that communicates an intention and can be made with the time, space, materials and access available. A small original piece can work well.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and ten small planning spaces for two rough ideas each. Use a third space only if useful.
Optional visual route: six drawing tools including the adult model, five blank layout areas and a small set of colour tools for planning labels. No paint, cutting or fixing is required this week.
Sound or movement plans: five four-part sequence spaces, or five spoken/witness records. Fingertips and seated actions are enough for a brief planning demonstration.
Adult examples: two or three labelled original rough plans, one selected plan and one materials-and-time plan. These are teacher models, not pupil evidence.
For lesson two retain each pupil's chosen rough plan, reason and any feedback. No recording device or specialist art kit is required.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Point to the chosen rough plan. Say: I keep my idea and add labels so someone can follow it.
15 to 30 seconds
Label start, turn and new route. Say: I need one sheet and two colour tools. A silent sequence needs no art tools.
30 to 45 seconds
Say three ordered making steps. Show the draft forty-minute split: five set-up, twenty making, ten checking and five tidy.
45 to 60 seconds
Read the plan back and add one missing note. Say: This is a usable plan for later making, not a finished artwork.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Ask for one practical question about your plan. Decide what to keep or change and say why. Explain how your tools, time and access choices fit the idea. Set a check before making.
stretch.evidence: Keep the annotated plan, feedback, your decision with reasons, resource or access choices and the next check.
stretch.why_optional: This task is extra. Your Explore work is complete without it. Keep the record in case your next level changes.
stretch.good: The pupil evaluates whether the plan can communicate the intention under real constraints, explains a feedback decision and identifies a readiness check before making.
stretch.fallback: Adult reads the full oral plan back and retains the practical question, pupil's decision, reasons and next check in exact confirmed words.

models: Teacher model only: My plan shows a path finding another route. I labelled the turn, counted one sheet and two colour tools, and put my steps in order. I added a label after feedback. I still need the adult to approve the space.

Teacher model only: My silent piece has four parts: repeat, pause, change, return. I need no art tools. I chose small seated actions and a raised-hand stop. My draft time plan leaves time to practise and tidy.
lessons.cover: Recover the selected plan or make a short honest catch-up choice. Model labels, counted resources or no-tools access, ordered steps and a draft first making-period schedule. Pupils develop an annotated layout or ordered sequence, then use a private read-back to check it. Do not begin full making or claim completed artwork. Keep the plan for next week. Follow the seven-stage timing.
